extracted.intended_audience: aspiring standup comedians and writers who want to add comedic elements to their work
extracted.subtask_description: A practical five-step process for generating, expanding, ordering, pacing, and testing comedic material for standup and for applying humor to other forms of writing (stories, books, screenplays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with a funny topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by finding a subject or topic that strikes you as inherently funny or fertile for jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jerry described discovering the portable-toilet thread while discussing consoling someone over a death; a friend pointed out 'that's a funny area' and he developed five jokes from it. Advice: brainstorm ideas and topics you find interesting/funny and pursue them—whole chapters or books can grow from a single topic. Use everyday observations or conversational sparks as source material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think of emotions and images around the topic to generate jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the emotions and vivid images associated with the topic to create multiple joke angles rather than stating the obvious detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly: 'Think: How many jokes can you get out of a subject? Two to three is good; four to five is great; more and you're a master.' Example: in the portable-toilet set Jerry avoided directly mentioning human waste and instead mined hinges, dread, the interior feeling, and mental scarring. Techniques: emphasize relatability and surprise (e.g., 'What's the deal with that?') and use surprising imagery and emotional beats to increase material and make it relatable to audiences or readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble the jokes logically and connect them
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange individual jokes so they flow from one to another, connect to prior topics, and produce an overall coherent bit or scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jerry transitioned into portable-toilet jokes from a previous topic and arranged roughly five jokes so each flowed. If jokes are similar, space them apart: 'You can put separate similar jokes into two if you put space between them.' Consider ordering so the punchier joke lands later (e.g., place strongest joke at end), and use bookending—introduce an idea at the start and return to it at the end—to land additional laughs. Apply the same sequencing ideas to chapters/scenes in prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compress the jokes and adjust pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tighten and compress material so jokes come quickly after one another to build momentum and maximize laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jerry: 'The closer you can get the jokes together, the bigger the laughs will be. Compression is a very important aspect.' Goal is to trigger 'the roll'—deliver jokes rapidly so laughter compounds and audiences have less time to stop laughing. Compression keeps audiences loose and ready to laugh at succeeding lines. For writers, think about narrative pacing: putting comedic beats closer can increase perceived funniness of a scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test jokes in smaller groups and iterate
rubrics_metrics.description: Try material in low-stakes settings to see what works, gather feedback, and refine before presenting to larger audiences or publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jerry habitually showed up at small club shows to test new material (e.g., Gotham Comedy Club). For amateurs: test with friends/family, open mics, amateur shows. For writers: use editors or critique groups to read and respond before pitching/publishing. Use audience reactions to inform compression, ordering, and content choices.
